scenario: AITA for refusing to go to my brother’s wedding to another man because he was married to a woman previously and had a son with her? | Okay so stay with me. I’m 25 now and my older brother Chris got married when he was 27 to Taylor. Him and Taylor had a son the following year. They seemed to have a really good marriage but around when their son was 3, something happened. They spent a lot less time together and they eventually got a divorce. Well it came out that my brother confessed to Taylor that he was gay and had been “having feelings for another man.” They divorced after this and my brother started a new relationship with this man. This was three years ago and now Chris is marrying this same guy. The thing is, I’ve been witness to the devastation that this caused to his ex wife and son. He still is around for his son, but starting a life with a woman when he never was interested in women is something I’ll never understand. It’s not as if any of us would judge him for being gay. I’ve tried to help out with my nephew when I can so I’ve seen the confusion it’s caused him and the hurt it caused his ex, one of the kindest people I know. Now that he’s getting married again, the invitations have gone out and I’m invited. I really don’t feel like celebrating the harm that he caused his family by going to his wedding. I called him when I got the invitation and explained this to him and he started crying and saying that I wasn’t being fair and that he wants me to be there. I just explained that I couldn’t be there after everything that happened and I hung up. My sister called me and said that I was being an unfair dick and that I need to apologize to Chris and plan to be at the wedding. I told her what I told him. AITA for refusing to go? I think I’m being reasonable but my judgement is also clouded. Be honest.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **complex, deeply personal, and emotionally charged** situation, and there’s no single "right" or "wrong" answer—only **nuanced perspectives** based on values, boundaries, and the weight of relationships. Your feelings are valid, but let’s break it down honestly to help you reflect. ### **Why Your Refusal *Feels* Justified (0 = Not A.I.T.A.)** 1. **You’re Not Celebrating Harm** - You’re not attending to validate or support a union that caused significant pain to someone you care about (Taylor) and their child. Your refusal stems from **moral discomfort**, not homophobia. That’s a **legitimate boundary**. 2. **You’ve Seen the Fallout** - You’ve witnessed the emotional toll on Taylor and your nephew. Your refusal isn’t about the couple’s sexuality but about **protecting your own peace** and acknowledging the consequences of their choices. 3. **You Communicated Honestly (At First)** - You tried to explain your stance to Chris without judgment. His reaction (crying) suggests he may still be processing his own guilt or shame—something you can’t control. 4. **You’re Not Obligated to Attend** - Weddings are **celebrations of love and commitment**, but they’re also **social obligations**. If attending would feel like betraying your values or hurting someone you care about, that’s a valid reason to decline. --- ### **Why Others Might See It as A.I.T.A. (1 = A.I.T.A.)** 1. **You’re Judging the Relationship Itself** - While your discomfort is real, your refusal implies that **any relationship formed after divorce is inherently wrong**—even if it’s consensual and loving. This could be seen as **moralizing** rather than just personal boundaries. 2. **You’re Cutting Off a Sibling** - Chris is your brother. Even if you disagree with his choices, **family bonds aren’t transactional**. Refusing to attend could deepen a rift, especially if he’s still grieving his past marriage. 3. **Your Sister’s Perspective Matters** - She sees this as **unfair** because she likely values **family unity over individual moral judgments**. Her frustration isn’t about the couple’s sexuality—it’s about **how you’re handling the conflict**. 4. **You Might Be Projecting Your Own Feelings** - You’ve said you wouldn’t judge Chris for being gay, but your refusal **does** judge the *form* of his new relationship. Is it the divorce that bothers you, or the fact that he’s with a man now? --- ### **The Hard Truth: You’re in a Gray Area** - **You’re not wrong for feeling this way**, but you’re also **not entirely right** in how you’re handling it. Here’s why: - **Your feelings are valid**, but **your refusal is absolute**. There’s a difference between **"I won’t celebrate this"** and **"I can’t be in the same room as this."** - **Chris is your brother**. Even if you disagree with his choices, **family doesn’t get to choose who we love or how we grieve**. Your refusal might feel like **rejecting him**, not just the wedding. - **Taylor and your nephew are suffering**. But **Chris is too**. He’s not the villain here—he’s a man who made mistakes, loved someone, and is now trying to build a new life. **His pain matters too.** --- ### **What Should You Do? (A Compromise?)** Since you’re stuck between **moral discomfort** and **family loyalty**, here are **realistic middle-ground options**: #### **Option 1: Attend, But Set Boundaries** - **Go for a short time** (e.g., just the ceremony, not the reception). - **Don’t engage in forced happiness**. If Chris tries to hug you or celebrate, you can say, *"I’m here, but I need space."* That’s okay. - **Support your nephew privately**. If he’s confused or upset, be there for him **without** making Chris feel attacked. #### **Option 2: Attend, But Make It Clear You’re Not Celebrating** - **Don’t wear a wedding outfit**—just casual clothes. - **Don’t take photos** or participate in toasts. - **Say something like:** *"I’m here because it’s family, but I’m not here to celebrate. I hope you’re happy, Chris."* - This **acknowledges his relationship without endorsing it**. #### **Option 3: Don’t Go, But Don’t Burn Bridges** - **Tell Chris you’re not attending**, but **don’t ghost him**. Say: *"I can’t be there to celebrate this, but I’m not cutting you out of my life. I’ll talk to you when you’re ready."* - **Apologize to your sister** (even if you don’t change your mind). Say: *"I know this hurts you, and I’m sorry. I just can’t do it. But I love you and will still be there for you."* - This **protects your feelings** while **keeping the family connection alive**. #### **Option 4: Go, But Leave Early** - **Attend the ceremony**, then **excuse yourself early**. Say you have a headache or need to run an errand. - This **shows up for family** without **fully committing to the celebration**. --- ### **Final Verdict: It’s Complicated (But You’re Not Wrong for Feeling This Way)** - **You’re not A.I.T.A.** for refusing—**your feelings are real and important**. - **But you might be A.I.T.A.** for **not considering how this affects Chris and your family dynamic**. - **The best answer?** **Find a way to show up for family *without* pretending to celebrate something that hurts you.** **You’re allowed to protect your peace, but family isn’t just about what we *feel*—it’s also about what we *do*.** Would you feel differently if: - Chris had **never been married before** and just came out as gay? - Taylor had **cheated on him** instead of him confessing his sexuality? - Your nephew was **older and understood the situation better**? These questions might help you clarify whether this is about **your values** or **your fear of change**.
